en: The Questions of King Milinda:
The Chapter on Similes, Section on Ants.
6. The Question of the Old Jackal “Venerable Nāgasena, when you say that ‘two qualities of the old jackal are to be adopted,’ which are those two qualities to be adopted?
“Great King, just as the old jackal, having obtained food, eats his fill without feeling disgust;”
In the same way, Great King, when a practitioner of yoga has obtained food, he should consume it without loathing, merely for the sake of sustaining the body.
This, Great King, is the first quality of the old jackal that should be adopted.
And this was said, Great King, by the Elder Mahākassapa:
Having descended from my lodging,
I entered the village for alms;
there I saw a man with leprosy eating.
I attended upon him with due respect.
With his hand still wet from washing,
he offered me a morsel of food.
While he was dropping in a morsel of food,
his finger was cut off right there against the base of the wall.
‘I ate that morsel;
whether while eating it or after having eaten,
no sense of disgust arose in me.’”
Furthermore, Great King, once an old jackal has obtained food, it does not discriminate between whether it is coarse or refined;

even so, Great King, a practitioner who is a yogin, having obtained food, should not discriminate, thinking, ‘Is it coarse or refined, well-prepared or poorly prepared? He should be content with whatever he receives.
This, Great King, is the second quality to be adopted from the old jackal.
This was also said, Great King, by the Elder Upasena Vaṅganta-putta:
“One should be content even with what is coarse,
and not long for any other abundant flavor.”
The mind of one who is greedily attached to flavors does not delight in meditation; being satisfied with this or that,
he does not find joy in the higher states.
“He fulfills the state of a recluse.
Thus ends the sixth inquiry, the Question of the Old Jackal.
